cor-cnt-independence.title: The independence model
cor-cnt-independence.html:
Under @eq-cnt-independence the conditional distribution of the column given the row does not depend on the row, so the two classifications are independent. The maximum likelihood fitted values are μ^ij=yi+y+jn,yi+=∑jyij,y+j=∑iyij,n=y++,{#eq-cnt-independence-fit}

the deviance is G2=2∑i,jyijlog⁡(yij/μ^ij), the Pearson statistic is X2=∑i,j(yij−μ^ij)2/μ^ij, and both have (r−1)(c−1) residual degrees of freedom — and, when the expected counts are large, both are asymptotically χ2 on that many degrees of freedom (@thm-glm-deviance).

def-cnt-negbin.title: Negative binomial regression
def-cnt-negbin.html:
Let Y1,…,Yn be independent with the mass function @eq-cnt-nb-pmf, means μi and shapes κi, and let 𝛃log⁡μi=x(i)⊤β.

  1. The NB2 model takes κi=κ constant, so that Var(Yi)=μi+μi2κ.{#eq-cnt-nb2-variance}

    The variance is quadratic in the mean, and the coefficient of variation of Λi is the constant κ−1/2.

  2. The NB1 model takes κi=αμi proportional to the mean, so that Var(Yi)=μi+μiα=ϕμi,ϕ=1+α−1.{#eq-cnt-nb1-variance}

    The variance is linear in the mean, with a constant inflation factor.

The parameter α=1/κ in the NB2 model is often called the dispersion parameter; α=0 is the Poisson.

def-cnt-poisson.title: The Poisson log-linear model
def-cnt-poisson.html: Let Y1,…,Yn be independent, with Yi Poisson distributed with mean μi>0, and let x(i) be the ith row of a model matrix X of full column rank p. The Poisson log-linear model is the generalized linear model (@def-glm-model) with this random component, the log link and the linear predictor 𝛃ηi=x(i)⊤β: 𝛃𝛃log⁡μi=x(i)⊤β,equivalentlyμi=exp⁡(x(i)⊤β)=eβ1xi1⋯eβpxip.{#eq-cnt-model}

def-cnt-zero-models.title: Zero-inflated and hurdle models
def-cnt-zero-models.html:
Let f(y;λ) be a count distribution with parameter λ, such as the Poisson or the NB2 family of @def-cnt-negbin, and let z(i) and x(i) be rows of two model matrices, which may be equal, overlapping or disjoint.

  1. The zero-inflated model gives Yi the mass function Pr(Yi=y)={πi+(1−πi)f(0;λi),y=0,(1−πi)f(y;λi),y=1,2,…,{#eq-cnt-zip}

    with 𝛄logitπi=z(i)⊤γ and 𝛃log⁡λi=x(i)⊤β. Equivalently, a latent indicator Zi is one with probability πi, and Yi=0 when Zi=1 while Yi∼f(⋅;λi) when Zi=0. Taking f Poisson gives the zero-inflated Poisson (ZIP), and f negative binomial the zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB).

  2. The hurdle model gives Yi the mass function Pr(Yi=y)={1−ρi,y=0,ρif(y;λi)1−f(0;λi),y=1,2,…,{#eq-cnt-hurdle}

    with 𝛄logitρi=z(i)⊤γ and 𝛃log⁡λi=x(i)⊤β: a binary model decides whether the count is positive, and a zero-truncated version of f decides how large it is.

exm-cnt-exposure.title: Three ways to handle an exposure
exm-cnt-exposure.title_html: Three ways to handle an exposure
exm-cnt-exposure.html:
Counts are generated for m=300 units from log⁡μi=0.4+0.5xi+ψlog⁡ti, with xi standard normal and the exposure ti correlated with it. Three analyses are run on each of 2000 data sets — the correct offset, a free coefficient on log⁡t, and no exposure term — and Figure 37.2.1 shows the sampling distributions of the estimated slope of x, whose true value is 0.5.

When the truth is ψ=1, both the offset and the free-coefficient model are unbiased, with means 0.500 and 0.500, but the free coefficient has standard deviation 0.029 against 0.017, a loss of precision by a factor of 1.772: estimating a parameter you already know costs information. Dropping the exposure is a disaster, the slope averaging 1.096, because x is left to explain the variation in exposure as well as in the rate.

When the truth is ψ=0.7, the free-coefficient model is still centred at 0.501, while the offset model, forcing a wrong proportionality, is centred at 0.322 — a bias of more than six of its own standard deviations. Fixing a coefficient you have got wrong costs more than estimating one you knew.

exm-cnt-grouping.title: Twenty thousand records in thirty-two rows
exm-cnt-grouping.title_html: Twenty thousand records in thirty-two rows
exm-cnt-grouping.html:
Take the physician-visit data of @exm-cnt-visits and keep only categorical regressors: the individual-deductible indicator, the three self-rated health indicators, and the chronic-disease score banded into four groups. There are 32 distinct covariate patterns, holding between 9 and 3832 person-years. Collapse the 20190 records to these rows, recording the total visits and the number of person-years in each, and fit the rate model with offset the log of the person-years. The coefficients agree with the person-level fit to fourteen decimal places, as @prp-cnt-offsets(c) promises.

Read as rates, a person-year in excellent health, in the lowest disease band and on a plan without an individual deductible, is expected to produce 1.9758 visits; an individual deductible multiplies that by 0.8247, poor self-rated health by 1.6875, and the highest disease band by 2.2621.

The grouped deviance is 665.60 on 24 degrees of freedom, and now the χ2 calibration applies, since the smallest fitted cell mean is 24.7. The model is rejected. Where does the misfit sit? The fitted model has main effects only, so its 24 residual degrees of freedom are the interactions among the three factors; adding every two-factor interaction among them, 23 parameters in all, drops the deviance to 106.87 on 9 degrees of freedom, a fall of 558.7 on 15. Five sixths of the misfit is therefore mean model, not variance function. What survives the repair — 106.87 on nine degrees of freedom, still far beyond any plausible χ2 — is the Poisson variance function, which Section 37.4 takes up.

exm-cnt-negbin.title: Negative binomial fits to the visit counts
exm-cnt-negbin.title_html: Negative binomial fits to the visit counts
exm-cnt-negbin.html:
Refit the model of @exm-cnt-visits with the NB2 distribution, alternating the weighted least squares step of @prp-cnt-negbin(b) with a one-dimensional solve for κ. The fit gives κ^=0.7637, that is α^=1.3094; at the overall mean of 2.860 visits the model’s variance is 13.574 against the Poisson’s 2.860. The maximized log-likelihood rises from −62737.33 to −43468.52, so the likelihood ratio statistic for H0:α=0 is 38537.6; the boundary correction of @prp-cnt-negbin(e) halves a p-value whose logarithm is about −19275. The score statistic @eq-cnt-score-test, from the Poisson fit alone, is 523.0.

What changes is inference. For the individual-deductible indicator the point estimate moves only from −0.2648 to −0.2475, but its standard error moves from 0.0102 to 0.0218, a factor of 2.125. Two other repairs agree: scaling the Poisson standard errors by ϕ^, with ϕ^=6.319 the Pearson statistic over its degrees of freedom, gives 0.0257, and the sandwich estimator of @thm-het-sandwich gives 0.0268. A Poisson analysis would have declared effects significant on the strength of a variance assumption the data reject.

Fitting NB1 instead gives log-likelihood −43380.59 with ϕ^=4.766, a better fit than NB2 by AIC: 86779.2 against 86955.0, with the Poisson far behind at 125490.7. Figure 37.4.1 shows why the comparison is close. Sorting the person-years by fitted mean into twenty-five bins, the bin variances follow the NB2 curve at the high end, while in the crowded low range, where most of the data and most of the likelihood sit, NB1 is closer. AIC weighs the whole likelihood and the figure the upper tail; when they disagree, choose by the use the model will be put to.

exm-cnt-party.title: Education and party identification
exm-cnt-party.html:
The 1996 American National Election Studies sample distributed with statsmodels records 944 respondents. Cross-classify them by education in four levels (no diploma, high school graduate, some college, degree) and by party identification collapsed to three, with column totals 380, 239 and 325.

Fitting the independence model @cor-cnt-independence gives G2=20.541 and X2=19.338 on six degrees of freedom. The smallest expected count is 16.46, so the χ2 calibration is safe, and the p-value is 0.0022: independence is rejected. The largest Pearson residual (yij−μ^ij)/μ^ij is −2.62, at Republicans without a diploma, where 10 were observed against 22.38 expected; the largest positive one, 2.31, is at Democrats in the same row.

The alternative need not be saturated. Education is ordered, so give it scores ui=1,2,3,4 and fit log⁡μij=λ+λiR+λjC+uiδj, spending two parameters instead of six on the association. Its deviance is 7.367 on four degrees of freedom, p-value 0.1177: this model fits, and the drop from independence is 13.174 on two degrees of freedom, p=0.00138.

Now read the same three fits as multinomial logit models for party given education (@def-mlt-baseline), with Democrat as the baseline: independence becomes the intercept-only logit model, the score model a logit model linear in ui, the saturated model a logit model with a free effect per education level. Each pair gives identical fitted counts, and the association parameters δj are exactly the education slopes of the logit model, 0.1513 for Independent against Democrat and 0.2748 for Republican against Democrat: each step up the education scale multiplies the odds of Republican rather than Democrat by 1.3163. In the saturated model the interaction contrast comparing the degree row with the no-diploma row and the Republican column with the Democrat column is 1.3658, so those odds are 3.919 times as large among respondents with a degree as among those without a diploma.

exm-cnt-visits.title: Physician visits in a health insurance experiment
exm-cnt-visits.title_html: Physician visits in a health insurance experiment
exm-cnt-visits.html:
The RAND Health Insurance Experiment sample distributed with statsmodels records 20190 person-years. The response is the number of outpatient physician visits in the year, with mean 2.860 and a variance 7.093 times as large; @exm-lm-counts used the same data to show how badly a normal linear model describes it.

Fit @eq-cnt-model with an intercept, the logarithm of one plus the coinsurance rate (lncoins), an indicator of an individual-deductible plan (idp), a physical-limitation index, a chronic-disease score, and three indicators of self-rated health (good, fair, poor, against excellent). Fisher scoring converges in 7 steps. The coefficient of lncoins is −0.0712, standard error 0.0022: a rate ratio of 0.9313 per unit, Wald interval (0.9272,0.9354). Moving across its whole range of 4.615, from free care to the highest coinsurance plan, multiplies expected visits by 0.720. The disease score is not a count of diseases but a continuous index running to 58.6; each unit of it multiplies expected visits by 1.0353, so moving from its lower quartile 6.90 to its upper quartile 13.73 multiplies them by 1.267. Poor self-rated health multiplies them by 1.2441 against excellent health. The fitted counts sum to the observed total, and within each health group to that group’s total, as @thm-cnt-marginals requires.

exm-cnt-zeros.title: Five models for the physician visits
exm-cnt-zeros.title_html: Five models for the physician visits
exm-cnt-zeros.html:
A proportion 0.3124 of the 20190 person-years record no physician visit; the Poisson model of @exm-cnt-visits predicts 0.0809.

Table 37.5.1. Five count models for the physician-visit data, all with the same eight regressors; the zero-inflated models use them in both parts. The observed proportion of zeros is 0.3124.

model parameters log-likelihood AIC BIC fitted Pr(Y=0)
Poisson 8 −62737.3 125490.7 125554.0 0.0809
NB2 9 −43468.5 86955.0 87026.3 0.3200
ZIP 16 −54978.6 109989.1 110115.8 0.3125
ZINB 17 −43391.8 86817.5 86952.0 0.3255
hurdle NB 17 −43244.6 86523.2 86657.7 0.3124

Three things stand out. First, zero inflation alone does not save the Poisson: the ZIP reproduces the zeros almost exactly, at 0.3125, and still trails the plain negative binomial by more than eleven thousand in log-likelihood, because the trouble here is the whole shape of the distribution and not only its zeros. Second, the negative binomial already matches the zeros, at 0.3200 against 0.3124, as @exr-cnt-nb-limit predicts: heterogeneity in the rate produces excess zeros as a by-product, and adding zero inflation gains 153.5 in twice the log-likelihood for eight parameters while slightly overshooting, at 0.3255. Third, the hurdle model wins on both AIC and BIC, and by construction reproduces the zero proportion exactly.

The hurdle model wins because of the positive counts, not the zeros. Splitting each log-likelihood at y=0 shows it: on the zeros the hurdle model scores −6966.1 against the ZINB’s −6757.5, a loss of 208.6; on the positive counts −36278.5 against −36634.2, a gain of 355.7, for a net 147.2. Above two visits the two are indistinguishable in Figure 37.5.1; the difference is in how mass is arranged over the small positive counts, and the hurdle model buys that freedom by giving the truncated component its own shape, κ^=0.557 against 0.838 in the ZINB. Estimated zero inflation in the ZINB averages only 0.0475: it too spends its extra parameters re-shaping the low counts, which is what a hurdle model does directly.

exr-cnt-anscombe.title: B3
exr-cnt-anscombe.html: For a Poisson fit the Pearson residual is riP=(yi−μ^i)/μ^i. Show that it is strongly skewed when μi is small, and that the Anscombe residual 32(yi2/3−μ^i2/3)/μ^i1/6 has variance about one, by applying the delta method to Y2/3.

exr-cnt-conditional.title: B2
exr-cnt-conditional.html: For the conditional independence model log⁡μijk=λ+λiA+λjB+λkC+λikAC+λjkBC, show that the likelihood equations equate the AC and BC margins, that μ^ijk=yi+ky+jk/y++k, and that the residual degrees of freedom are (r−1)(c−1)ℓ for an r×c×ℓ table.

exr-cnt-df-count.title: A1
exr-cnt-df-count.html: A three-way table is 3×4×2. How many cells does it have, how many free parameters does the homogeneous association model have, and what are the residual degrees of freedom?

exr-cnt-em-monotone.title: B4
exr-cnt-em-monotone.html: Show that the EM step described around @eq-cnt-em-estep increases the observed-data log-likelihood at every iteration, by writing the observed-data log-likelihood as the expected complete-data log-likelihood minus an entropy term and using Jensen’s inequality.

exr-cnt-existence-check.title: C2
exr-cnt-existence-check.html: Give a data set with n=4, p=2 for which the condition of @prp-cnt-existence fails. Then add a ridge penalty 𝛃λ‖β‖2 (@def-shr-ridge) and show that the penalized log-likelihood has a finite maximizer for every λ>0.

exr-cnt-grouping-general.title: C1
exr-cnt-grouping-general.html: Extend @prp-cnt-offsets(c) to the case where the individual records already carry exposures ti that differ within a group. Show that the grouped fit with exposure ∑i∈gti reproduces the individual fit, and identify exactly what has to be constant within a group.

exr-cnt-hurdle-nests.title: C1
exr-cnt-hurdle-nests.html: Take f Poisson, z(i)=x(i), and a hurdle model whose binary part uses the complementary log–log link, 𝛄log⁡{−log⁡(1−ρi)}=z(i)⊤γ, in place of the logit of @def-cnt-zero-models(b). Show that this model contains the plain Poisson as the submodel 𝛄𝛃γ=β, so that a likelihood ratio test of the Poisson against it is a standard interior test on p restrictions, unlike the zero-inflated comparison of @prp-cnt-zero-inflation(d). Then show that the same is not true if the binary part uses the logit.

exr-cnt-identification.title: B3
exr-cnt-identification.html: Fit a ZINB to the physician-visit data using only an intercept in the inflation part, and compare its AIC with the model of @exm-cnt-zeros that uses all the regressors in both parts. Which does AIC prefer, and what does the comparison say about the eight inflation coefficients?

exr-cnt-identity-link.title: C1
exr-cnt-identity-link.html: Consider a Poisson model with the identity link, 𝛃μi=x(i)⊤β. Show that the log-likelihood is concave on the open set where every μi>0, but that the maximum can occur on its boundary, where some μ^i=0; what happens then to the standard errors an algorithm that ignores the constraint reports? Repeat for the additive rate model 𝛃μi=tix(i)⊤β of Section 37.2, whose coefficients are rate differences: show that its likelihood equations are ∑iti(yi−μi)x(i)/μi=0, and say why an epidemiologist asking how many events an intervention prevents wants it.

exr-cnt-independence-hand.title: B1
exr-cnt-independence-hand.html: For the 2×2 table with entries y11,y12,y21,y22, compute the independence fit @eq-cnt-independence-fit by hand and show that yij−μ^ij=±(y11y22−y12y21)/n with alternating signs. Deduce that X2=n(y11y22−y12y21)2/(y1+y2+y+1y+2).

exr-cnt-intercept-only.title: A2
exr-cnt-intercept-only.html: Show directly from @thm-cnt-score that in the model with an intercept only, the maximum likelihood estimate of the common mean is y¯, and that the deviance equals 2∑iyilog⁡(yi/y¯).

exr-cnt-logit-equivalence.title: B3
exr-cnt-logit-equivalence.html: In a 2×c×ℓ table with A binary, show that the homogeneous association model implies that the logit of Pr(A=1∣B=j,C=k) is additive in j and k, and identify the logistic regression that corresponds to it. Which log-linear terms determine the logistic intercept, which the slopes, and which do not appear at all?

exr-cnt-marginal-effects.title: C2
exr-cnt-marginal-effects.html: In a zero-inflated model βj is a log rate ratio for the count component, not for the response. Derive ∂log⁡E(Yi)/∂xij when xj appears in both parts, and explain why reporting eβ^j as “the effect on the expected count” is wrong.

exr-cnt-nb-canonical.title: C2
exr-cnt-nb-canonical.html: @prp-cnt-negbin(a) identifies the canonical link of the NB2 family as θ=log⁡{μ/(μ+κ)}. Work out the likelihood equations under this link, show that they take the form 𝛍X⊤(y−μ)=0, and explain why the log link is nevertheless the standard choice.

exr-cnt-nb-deviance.title: B4
exr-cnt-nb-deviance.html: Show that the deviance (@def-glm-deviance) of the NB2 model with κ known is D=2∑i=1n{yilog⁡yiμ^i−(yi+κ)log⁡yi+κμ^i+κ}, and that it tends to the Poisson deviance @eq-cnt-deviance as κ→∞. Why does an analysis of deviance based on it need κ to be held fixed across the models compared?

exr-cnt-nb-limit.title: B2
exr-cnt-nb-limit.html: Show that if Y is NB2 with mean μ and shape κ, then Pr(Y=0)=(1+μ/κ)−κ, that this exceeds e−μ for every finite κ, and that it tends to one as κ→0 with μ fixed. Interpret the last statement.

exr-cnt-offset-misspecified.title: C2
exr-cnt-offset-misspecified.html: Let the truth be log⁡μi=ψlog⁡ti+β0+β1xi with ψ≠1, and suppose the offset model is fitted. Show that the limiting value of β^1 solves E{xt(tψ−1eβ0+β1x−eβ0∗+β1∗x)}=0, and argue that β1∗=β1 when tψ−1 is independent of x under the weighting by t.

exr-cnt-offset-power.title: B2
exr-cnt-offset-power.html: In the setting of @exm-cnt-exposure, suppose the analyst tests H0:ψ=1 and uses the offset model if the test does not reject. Explain why the resulting estimator of the slope of x has a sampling distribution that is neither of the two shown in Figure 37.2.1, and relate the phenomenon to the pre-test problem @exm-sel-pretest-coverage.

exr-cnt-offset-units.title: A1
exr-cnt-offset-units.html: A rate model uses person-years as the exposure. A colleague re-expresses exposure in person-months, multiplying every ti by twelve. Which coefficients change and by how much? Which fitted values change?

exr-cnt-offset-vs-rate.title: A2
exr-cnt-offset-vs-rate.html: Explain why regressing log⁡(yi/ti) on x(i) by least squares is not equivalent to fitting @eq-cnt-offset, giving two distinct reasons.

exr-cnt-one-way.title: B1
exr-cnt-one-way.html: Counts yij, j=1,…,ni, are observed in c groups, and the model is log⁡μij=βi, one parameter per group. Show that μ^ij=y¯i⋅, that Var^(β^i)=1/(niy¯i⋅), and that a Wald interval for μh/μi is exp⁡{β^h−β^i±z1/(nhy¯h⋅)+1/(niy¯i⋅)}.

exr-cnt-one-way-lrt.title: B2
exr-cnt-one-way-lrt.html: In the setting of @exr-cnt-one-way, show that the likelihood ratio statistic for H0:μ1=⋯=μc is 2∑iniy¯i⋅log⁡(y¯i⋅/y¯), where y¯ is the overall mean, and state the conditions under which its χ2(c−1) calibration is reasonable.

exr-cnt-piecewise.title: B1
exr-cnt-piecewise.html: Suppose subject i is followed until an event or censoring, with a hazard that is constant at 𝛃hik=exp⁡(αk+x(i)⊤β) on interval k. Write dik∈{0,1} for the event indicator and tik for the time at risk in that interval. Show that the likelihood contribution of subject i is ∏khikdike−hiktik, and hence that maximizing it is the same as fitting a Poisson log-linear model to the dik with offset log⁡tik.

exr-cnt-poisson-sum.title: A2
exr-cnt-poisson-sum.html: Verify from @thm-cnt-poisson-multinomial(a) that the conditional distribution of Y1 given N=n is binomial with n trials and probability μ1/μ+, and use it to explain why a Poisson model for two counts is the same as a binomial model for one of them given the total.

exr-cnt-quasi-vs-nb.title: B3
exr-cnt-quasi-vs-nb.html: Show that the quasi-Poisson estimating equation for 𝛃β is the same as the Poisson one, so that 𝛃β^ is unchanged, while the NB2 equation @eq-cnt-nb-score downweights observations with large fitted means. Which model would you expect to be more affected by a single very large count?

exr-cnt-score-hand.title: B1
exr-cnt-score-hand.html: For an intercept-only Poisson model, μ^i=y¯ for every i. Show that the score statistic @eq-cnt-score-test reduces to n/2{sn2/y¯−1} with sn2=n−1∑i(yi−y¯)2, so that it compares the sample variance with the sample mean. Evaluate it for n=100, y¯=3, sn2=5.

exr-cnt-three-way.title: C2
exr-cnt-three-way.html: For a three-way table, show that the likelihood equations of the mutual independence model are μ^i++=yi++, μ^+j+=y+j+ and μ^++k=y++k, and solve them to get μ^ijk=yi++y+j+y++k/n2. Explain why the homogeneous association model has no such closed form.

exr-cnt-truncated.title: B1
exr-cnt-truncated.html: Let Y be Poisson with mean λ, truncated to {1,2,…}. Show that EY=λ/(1−e−λ) and VarY=EY{1+λ−EY}, and deduce that the truncated distribution is underdispersed relative to its own mean.

exr-cnt-underdispersion.title: C1
exr-cnt-underdispersion.html: Construct a count distribution with mean μ and variance strictly less than μ, and explain why no member of the negative binomial family has this property. What mechanisms produce underdispersed counts in practice, and what would you fit?

exr-cnt-uniform-association.title: C1
exr-cnt-uniform-association.html: The model of @exm-cnt-party with row scores, log⁡μij=λ+λiR+λjC+uiδj, is called a row-effects model. Show that its local log odds ratios log⁡{μijμi+1,j+1/(μi,j+1μi+1,j)} equal (ui+1−ui)(δj+1−δj). Then show that giving both classifications scores, with association term θuivj, makes every local log odds ratio θ(ui+1−ui)(vj+1−vj) — the uniform association model — and count its parameters.

exr-cnt-units.title: A1
exr-cnt-units.html: A Poisson log-linear model for the number of insurance claims has coefficient 0.182 on an indicator of urban residence. State the effect on the expected number of claims in words, and give the multiplicative effect of the indicator on the odds that a policy has at least one claim under the same model. Why is the second quantity not simply e0.182?

exr-cnt-variance-ratio.title: A1
exr-cnt-variance-ratio.html: A negative binomial NB2 fit reports κ^=2. By what factor does the model inflate the variance over the Poisson at a fitted mean of 1, of 10, and of 100? Repeat for an NB1 fit with ϕ^=3, and comment.

exr-cnt-why-not-chisq.title: A2
exr-cnt-why-not-chisq.html: A colleague reports a likelihood ratio statistic of 2.9 for Poisson against NB2 and, comparing with χ2(1), obtains p=0.089 and concludes there is no overdispersion. What is the correct p-value, and does the conclusion change at the five per cent level?

exr-cnt-zinb-vs-nb.title: B2
exr-cnt-zinb-vs-nb.html: Derive the mean and variance of a ZINB with inflation probability π, count mean λ and shape κ. Show that for a given mean and variance there is a curve of (π,λ,κ) values giving the same first two moments, and explain what this implies for the precision of the estimates.

exr-cnt-zip-mean.title: A1
exr-cnt-zip-mean.html: A ZIP model has π=0.3 and λ=4. Compute EY, VarY, Pr(Y=0) and the ratio of variance to mean, and compare with a Poisson having the same mean.

lem-cnt-gamma-mixture.title: The negative binomial as a gamma mixture of Poissons
lem-cnt-gamma-mixture.title_html: The negative binomial as a gamma mixture of Poissons
lem-cnt-gamma-mixture.html:
Let Λ have the gamma distribution with shape κ>0 and rate κ/μ, so that EΛ=μ and VarΛ=μ2/κ, and let Y∣Λ=λ be Poisson with mean λ. Then:

  1. more generally, for any mixing distribution with EΛ=μ and VarΛ=τ2, EY=μ and VarY=μ+τ2;

  2. with the gamma mixing distribution above, the marginal mass function of Y is Pr(Y=y)=Γ(y+κ)Γ(κ)y!(κκ+μ)κ(μκ+μ)y,y=0,1,2,…{#eq-cnt-nb-pmf}

    with EY=μ and VarY=μ+μ2/κ;

  3. as κ→∞ with μ fixed, @eq-cnt-nb-pmf converges to the Poisson mass function with mean μ.

prp-cnt-existence.title: Existence of the maximum likelihood estimate
prp-cnt-existence.title_html: Existence of the maximum likelihood estimate
prp-cnt-existence.html: Let rank(X)=p. The log-likelihood @eq-cnt-loglik attains its maximum at a finite 𝛃β^ if and only if there is no vector d≠0 with x(i)⊤d≤0  for every i,andx(i)⊤d=0  whenever yi>0.{#eq-cnt-divergent}

prp-cnt-interaction.title: Interaction parameters are log odds ratios
prp-cnt-interaction.title_html: Interaction parameters are log odds ratios
prp-cnt-interaction.html: In @eq-cnt-saturated, for any rows i≠k and columns j≠l, λijRC+λklRC−λilRC−λkjRC=log⁡μijμklμilμkj, which does not depend on the side conditions (@thm-est-side-conditions) used to identify the parameters. Under the multinomial reading of @thm-cnt-poisson-multinomial the right-hand side is the log odds ratio log⁡{πijπkl/(πilπkj)}. The model @eq-cnt-independence holds if and only if every such quantity is zero.

prp-cnt-negbin.title: Fitting the negative binomial
prp-cnt-negbin.html:
In the NB2 model of @def-cnt-negbin with κ treated as a parameter:

  1. for fixed κ the distribution @eq-cnt-nb-pmf is an exponential dispersion family (@def-glm-edf) with natural parameter θ=log⁡{μ/(μ+κ)}, cumulant function b(θ)=−κlog⁡(1−eθ), dispersion ϕ=1 and variance function V(μ)=μ+μ2/κ;

  2. with the log link, the score for 𝛃β is 𝛃∂ℓ∂β=∑i=1nyi−μi1+μi/κx(i),{#eq-cnt-nb-score}

    so that Fisher scoring is iteratively reweighted least squares with weights wi=μi/(1+μi/κ), and the expected information for 𝛃β is X⊤WX;

  3. 𝛃β and κ are orthogonal: 𝛃E{∂2ℓ/∂β∂κ}=0. Hence the asymptotic distribution of 𝛃β^ is the same whether κ is known or estimated, and the two can be updated alternately;

  4. the score for κ is ∑i{ψ(yi+κ)−ψ(κ)+log⁡κκ+μi+1−κ+yiκ+μi}, where ψ is the digamma function; it has no closed-form root and is solved numerically;

  5. the Poisson model is the boundary case α=1/κ=0. The likelihood ratio statistic L for H0:α=0 is therefore not asymptotically χ2(1); under the conditions of Self and Liang (1987) its limiting distribution is 12χ2(0)+12χ2(1), so the p-value is Pr{N(0,1)>L}, half the naive one;

  6. in the NB1 model of @def-cnt-negbin(b), with κi=αμi and a log link, the score for 𝛃β at fixed α is 𝛃∂ℓ∂β=α∑i=1nμi{ψ(yi+αμi)−ψ(αμi)+log⁡α1+α}x(i).{#eq-cnt-nb1-score}

    The residual yi−μi does not appear, so this is not a weighted least squares equation at all. The quasi-Poisson model of Chapter 38 shares the NB1 variance function V(μ)=ϕμ but has the Poisson estimating equation 𝛍X⊤(y−μ)=0, so the two give different 𝛃β^ from the same data (@exr-cnt-quasi-vs-nb): a variance function does not determine a fit. Overdispersion is the rule rather than the exception, and modelling it changes the coefficients little and the standard errors a great deal; which of the three devices to use turns on whether a likelihood is needed, as it is for AIC and for Section 37.5.

prp-cnt-offsets.title: Offsets
prp-cnt-offsets.html:
Consider the model @eq-cnt-offset with rank(X)=p, and write 𝛍𝛍𝛃μ=μ(β) for the mean vector it defines. Then:

  1. the log-likelihood is 𝛃𝛃𝛃ℓ(β)=∑i{yi(log⁡ti+x(i)⊤β)−tiex(i)⊤β}−∑ilog⁡yi!; its score is 𝛍X⊤(y−μ) and its information is X⊤WX with W=diag(μ1,…,μn), so @thm-cnt-score holds verbatim with the offset in place;

  2. consequently @thm-cnt-marginals holds verbatim: the fitted counts, not the fitted rates, reproduce the observed margins of the model matrix, and with an intercept ∑iμ^i=∑iyi;

  3. (grouping) suppose the rows of X take only G distinct values x(g), with ng rows equal to the gth, all with exposure ti=1. Let sg be the total count of group g. Then fitting @eq-cnt-model to the n individual records and fitting @eq-cnt-offset to the G totals sg with exposures tg=ng give the same 𝛃β^, the same information matrix and the same deviance differences between nested models;

  4. (a free exposure coefficient) the model 𝛃log⁡μi=ψlog⁡ti+x(i)⊤β contains @eq-cnt-offset as the submodel ψ=1. Its fit coincides with the offset fit if and only if ψ^=1, and the likelihood ratio statistic for H0:ψ=1 is asymptotically χ2(1).

prp-cnt-zero-inflation.title: Properties of the two models
prp-cnt-zero-inflation.html:
In the notation of @def-cnt-zero-models, write μi=E(Yi) and 1i=1{yi>0}. The zero-inflated log-likelihood is ∑i:yi=0log⁡{πi+(1−πi)f(0;λi)}+∑i:yi>0[log⁡(1−πi)+log⁡f(yi;λi)],

and the hurdle one is ∑i[1ilog⁡ρi+(1−1i)log⁡(1−ρi)]+∑i:yi>0[log⁡f(yi;λi)−log⁡{1−f(0;λi)}].

Then:

  1. for the zero-inflated model with f Poisson, μi=(1−πi)λi,Var(Yi)=μi(1+πiλi),{#eq-cnt-zip-moments}

    so a zero-inflated Poisson is always overdispersed relative to its own mean unless πi=0;

  2. the hurdle log-likelihood separates, 𝛄𝛃𝛄𝛃ℓ(γ,β,⋅)=ℓbinary(γ)+ℓpositive(β,⋅), so the two parts can be fitted independently, and their estimates are asymptotically independent; the zero-inflated log-likelihood does not separate;

  3. the hurdle model can represent zero deflation, ρi>1−f(0;λi), while @eq-cnt-zip needs πi≥0 and can only add zeros; and, for the hurdle model, if z(i) contains an intercept then its fitted probabilities of a zero average to the observed proportion of zeros, whatever else is in the binary part. The zero-inflated model satisfies no such identity;

  4. the zero-inflated model contains f itself as the limiting case πi≡0, which lies outside the range where the usual expansion is valid, so a likelihood ratio test of f against its zero-inflated version is not asymptotically χ2; nor is the Vuong statistic of @eq-cnt-vuong valid for such a comparison.

thm-cnt-dispersion-score.title: Score test against NB2 alternatives
thm-cnt-dispersion-score.html:
Let μ^i be the fitted means of a Poisson log-linear model with rank(X)=p, and consider the NB2 family @eq-cnt-nb-alpha indexed by α≥0. Then the score for α at α=0 is ∂ℓ∂α|α=0=12∑i=1n{(yi−μi)2−yi},{#eq-cnt-score-alpha}

its variance under the Poisson model is 12∑iμi2, and its covariance with the score for 𝛃β is zero. Suppose in addition that, as n→∞ with p fixed, the true means stay in a fixed compact interval inside (0,∞) and no observation dominates, in the sense that ∑i=1nμi4(∑i=1nμi2)2⟶0.{#eq-cnt-score-lyapunov}

Then S=∑i=1n{(yi−μ^i)2−yi}2∑i=1nμ^i2{#eq-cnt-score-test}

is asymptotically standard normal under the Poisson model, and the test rejects for large positive S.

thm-cnt-marginals.title: Fitted values reproduce observed margins
thm-cnt-marginals.html:
Let 𝛍μ^ solve the likelihood equations of @thm-cnt-score. Then 𝛍xj⊤μ^=xj⊤y for every column xj of X, and more generally 𝛍a⊤μ^=a⊤y for every a∈C(X). In particular:

  1. if the model has an intercept, the fitted counts sum to the observed total, ∑iμ^i=∑iyi;

  2. if X contains the indicator of a group G, the fitted counts of that group sum to its observed total, ∑i∈Gμ^i=∑i∈Gyi;

  3. if X contains a quantitative regressor xj, the fitted counts reproduce the observed xj-weighted total.

thm-cnt-poisson-multinomial.title: Poisson counts conditioned on their total
thm-cnt-poisson-multinomial.title_html: Poisson counts conditioned on their total
thm-cnt-poisson-multinomial.html:
1. Let Y1,…,Yc be independent, Yj Poisson with mean μj>0, and N=∑jYj. Then N is Poisson with mean μ+=∑jμj, and conditionally on N=n the vector (Y1,…,Yc) is multinomial with n trials and probabilities πj=μj/μ+.

  2. Suppose the cells are indexed by a stratum s=1,…,S and a category j=1,…,c, the counts Ysj are independent Poisson with means μsj, and the log-linear model is 𝛄log⁡μsj=αs+zsj⊤γ,{#eq-cnt-strata}

    with 𝛂α∈RS unrestricted: that is, the model contains a free parameter for every stratum. Then the Poisson log-likelihood splits as 𝛂𝛄𝛄ℓ(α,γ)=ℓ1(μ1+,…,μS+)+ℓ2(γ)+constant, where ℓ1 is the log-likelihood of S independent Poisson totals and ℓ2 is the log-likelihood of S independent multinomial samples with category probabilities 𝛄𝛄𝛄πsj(γ)=exp⁡(zsj⊤γ)∑l=1cexp⁡(zsl⊤γ),{#eq-cnt-multinomial-pi}

    and the two pieces have no parameters in common.

  3. Consequently the maximum likelihood estimate 𝛄γ^ from the Poisson fit is the maximum likelihood estimate from the multinomial fit; the fitted cell counts are μ^sj=nsπ^sj with ns=∑jysj; the observed information for 𝛄γ is the same in the two models; and deviance differences between models that all contain the stratum parameters agree. The stratum parameters α^s themselves have no multinomial counterpart: they are determined by μ^s+=ns.

thm-cnt-score.title: The Poisson likelihood equations
thm-cnt-score.html:
In the model of @def-cnt-poisson the log-likelihood is 𝛃𝛃𝛃ℓ(β)=∑i=1n{yix(i)⊤β−exp⁡(x(i)⊤β)}−∑i=1nlog⁡yi!,{#eq-cnt-loglik}

and, writing 𝛍𝛍𝛃μ=μ(β) for the vector of means and W=diag(μ1,…,μn):

  1. the score is 𝛃𝛍∂ℓ/∂β=X⊤(y−μ), so the likelihood equations are 𝛍X⊤(y−μ^)=0;

  2. the observed and expected information coincide and equal X⊤WX;

  3. ℓ is concave, and strictly concave when rank(X)=p, so a stationary point is the unique maximum.
